Football dashboard

The big five European leagues — plus Allsvenskan — under the hood: standings, xG team analytics, player profiles and second-order insights.

Big five 2026/27 · Allsvenskan 2026TheSportsDB + Understat + FotMobUpdated 2026-09-02 10:08 (Stockholm)

Names marked like this open something — a club, a player, a match. The address bar follows you, so any card can be linked to.

What's new · 2026-09-01

2026-09-01

  • Allsvenskan match reports now show where the shots came from. A pitch per team with a circle for every attempt, placed where it was struck and sized by how good a chance it was: green for a goal, blue for a save, grey for a block, hollow for a miss. Hover one for the player, the minute and what it was worth, or click it for their season card.
  • Allsvenskan match reports now show who played. Both squads under the stats, starters and substitutes, with FotMob's rating out of 10, minutes, goals, assists, expected goals and assists and shots for that match alone — and saves and goals prevented for the keepers. Click any name for that player's season card.

2026-08-31

  • Allsvenskan match reports now carry everything FotMob measured. Under the headline stats there's a new section with big chances, touches in the box, xG open play and set play, shots in and out of the box, passing, corners, tackles, blocks, clearances, saves, duels, fouls and cards. Rows nobody wins — the ones that climb simply because you spent the half defending — are drawn faint rather than awarded to anyone.
  • Match reports now show the full stat line. Pick a played match and the report gives you everything the feed stored for those 90 minutes — the big five get non-penalty xG, deep completions, PPDA and expected points beside the xG; Allsvenskan gets xG on target, shots, shots on target and possession too — each as two numbers with the bar between them.

2026-08-30

  • Every view has a link now. The address bar follows you — league, tab, match, the clubs in the comparison and the open player card — so you can copy the URL of exactly what you are looking at, and Back walks it. Names that open something are marked more clearly, with the rule stated once under the search box.
  • Player cards work from everywhere, and Allsvenskan players have them now. Opening a player from a club's squad list or from search showed nothing at all; percentiles early in a season read "NaNth". Both fixed — and an Allsvenskan squad name now opens a profile built from what FotMob publishes.
  • Search the whole dashboard from one box. Press / (or Ctrl-K, or the button under the badges) and type a club, a player or a section — every league at once. Enter opens the club card, the player's profile, or scrolls to the section.

2026-08-29

  • Club names are clickable across the Insights and Best of Europe tables too. The justice table, venue dependence and the continental justice table all open a club in Team analytics now — and from Best of Europe that switches league for you.
  • The xG table's club names are clickable. On Team analytics, clicking any club in the xG table loads it into the comparison card below — so you can move from one club to the next without going back to the dropdown.
  • The squad list says how many matches it covers. A club one matchday into the season shows sixteen players because sixteen have played — the heading now says so, rather than leaving a short list looking like missing data.
  • Club cards now show the squad. Pick a single club in Team analytics and you get everyone who has played for it, most minutes first, with goals against xG and assists against xA. In the big five, clicking a name opens that player's profile and career — so you can go from a league table to a club to a player without leaving the page.
  • Clearer clicking in the results tables. Club names are now underlined where they lead somewhere, and only the name itself opens the club — the rest of the row opens the match, as before. The note above each table says which is which.
  • Player profile cards now carry the player's whole career. Click any player in the explorer and under the percentile bars is every season Understat has stored for them -- club, minutes, goals against xG, assists against xA -- so transfers, breakout years and quiet ones read in one place. Seasons spent outside the big five are marked rather than skipped.
  • Every club now has a season-by-season history. Pick a single club in Team analytics and you get one row per season back to 2014/15 -- where they finished, the record, goal difference and xG difference, and points against expected points, with a bar showing which seasons banked more than the chances deserved and which banked fewer. Seasons spent in a lower division show as gaps, so promotions and relegations are visible too.

5 older entries are in CHANGELOG.md in the repository.

Predictions (xG Poisson model)

How to read this
Each club gets an attack and defence strength: a recency-weighted blend of 70% non-penalty xG and 30% actual goals, for and against (a match 180 days old counts half as much as one today — penalties are mostly noise, while real goals carry a club's persistent finishing skill). For a fixture, the home side's expected goals are its attack scaled by the opponent's defence relative to the league average, times a home-advantage factor measured from the league's own home/away xG split — and the same, mirrored, for the visitors. Feeding both expectations through independent Poisson distributions gives a probability for every scoreline, summed into the win/draw/win split shown in the bar. xG f'cast is each side's expected goals — deliberately not turned into a predicted scoreline, because chance quality says little about which exact score a match lands on and even the favourite scoreline rarely tops 15%. In the Understat leagues a small territory term also scales each attack by the club's deep-completions rate relative to the league average — validated on held-out seasons, unlike pressing intensity (PPDA), which was tried the same way, carried no extra signal, and stays out. Allsvenskan's feed has no deep-completions metric, so its model simply omits the term. Strengths reach back 1400 days — nearly four seasons — with that 180-day half-life doing the forgetting, a combination that beat a shorter hard-cutoff window on held-out seasons: an old match should fade, not fall off a cliff, because even faint evidence of how good a club is turns out to be worth keeping. Replaying every stored season with this exact recipe (backtest.py, 20,900 predictable matches) gives Brier 0.583 and 53% outcome accuracy, against 0.647 and 44% for guessing by league base rates.
A model, not a promise. These probabilities come from a small Poisson model over each club's recency-weighted chance quality (non-penalty xG, blended with a dash of actual goals) — nothing else. It has never heard of transfers, injuries, suspensions or new managers, and until the new season produces matches it leans heavily on last season's form. Clubs with no recent top-flight xG history at all have their fixtures left unpredicted. Backtested over 21,700 matches back to 2014/15 it calls the right result 53% of the time — clearly better than always guessing home win (44%), nowhere near clairvoyant. A conversation starter — never betting advice.

Season projection (2026-2027)

How to read this

What it does. Every fixture left in the season is played out 5,000 times using the same Poisson model as the predictions above, and the resulting final tables are counted up. Proj is the average final points total; the three percentages are how often a club finished first, in the top 4, and in the bottom 3.

Why it disagrees with the table. Points already banked are carried over untouched — they are real. Everything still to come is projected from recency-weighted non-penalty xG, which is mostly deaf to a hot finishing run. So a club sitting third on a thin xG record gets to keep its points and is still projected to fade, while a good side stuck in mid-table is projected to climb. The gap between the Now and # columns is that disagreement, in places.

Does it work? season_lab.py replays 58 finished seasons and projects the final table at ten points in each. Before a ball is kicked it lands 8.2 points per club from the final total; after a tenth of a season, 7.7 — against 18.8 for reading the table and multiplying, which at that stage is worse than simply assuming every club finishes on the league average. The model is ahead at every checkpoint right through to the final tenth, on held-out seasons its settings were never tuned on. Shrinking it back toward the table was tried and made it worse at every weight. Worth knowing: the preseason projection is already most of the way there. Updating it as results arrive is worth about 0.2 points per club after a tenth of the season, peaks near 0.7 at halfway, and is back under 0.2 by the run-in — most of what this table knows, it knew in August.

Reading the percentages. They are simulation frequencies, not certainties, and the top-four and bottom-three cuts are the site's own convention — real European and relegation places vary by league and by season. Anything under 0.5% shows as a dash.

Form, not news. The simulation knows only what clubs have done on the pitch. It has never heard of a transfer window, a sacking or an injury — when those things matter, they reach the projection the slow way, through results. It also assumes each club's current level holds for the rest of the season, which is exactly the assumption a January collapse breaks. A club returning after a year in the division below is projected on the last top-flight football it played, which may be a squad ago. A club scoring far more than its chances suggest is only partly credited for it — usually the right call, since across 1,170 historical team-seasons that kind of overperformance mostly evaporates, but the extreme cases (Sirius-scale runs included) regressed to roughly half their gap rather than to zero, and the model's discount was never tuned specifically for that tail.

360 of 380 matches left to play. Points already won are kept as they are; every remaining fixture is simulated from current xG form.

How wide is that projection?

How to read this

What it shows. The same 5,000 simulated seasons behind the Proj column above, but kept as a distribution of finishing positions instead of averaged down to one number. A short bar means the simulations agree; a long one means the run-in is still wide open for that club.

Reading it. The thick bar covers the middle half of simulated outcomes, the thin line the middle 90% — so a club whose thick bar sits entirely inside the shaded relegation band is in real trouble, while one whose bar straddles the line is still fighting it. The tick is the median finish, which is usually close to but not identical to the rounded Proj points figure above (points and rank are different simulation outputs).

Simulate one season

How to read this

What it does. Click the button and every fixture still to be played gets one simulated scoreline — each team's goals drawn from a Poisson distribution around the same expected-goals number (lam_home/lam_away) used everywhere else on this page — then the final table is built from real goals this time, not just win/draw/loss margins, so goal difference and the goals column are genuine tiebreakers rather than a coin flip. Click again for a different one.

Why it won't match the projection above. The Proj table is the average of thousands of these; any single run can and will put a mid-table side in the title race or drop a contender to mid-table, the same way any one real season can. That's the point of running it once instead of a thousand times — it shows what a plausible individual outcome actually looks like, not just the odds of it.

Plays every remaining fixture once, using the same expected-goals numbers as the projection above.

Projection over time

How to read this

What it shows. The season projection above is recomputed from scratch on every build, so on its own the page can only ever show tonight's opinion. This is every previous night's opinion too — one point added per team per night the projection ran, going back to the first snapshot logged this season.

Reading it. The number is projected final points, not the live table — it moves for two different reasons that look identical on the curve: a result banking real points, or the model simply revising its opinion of a club's remaining fixtures without a ball being kicked. Hover any dot for that night's title, European and relegation odds, which move for the same two reasons.

Why not just show probabilities. Title, European and relegation odds are usually a flat 0% or 100% for most of a season for most clubs — a true story for a handful of teams and a flat line for everyone else. Projected points moves for every club, contending or not, which is why it is the line and the odds are the hover.

One panel per team, today's projected order · 23 nightly snapshots logged so far · each panel is scaled to its own range, so a small club's swings are as visible as a title contender's — read the badge, not the height, for the size of the move · green = projection has risen since its first snapshot, red = fallen · hover a dot for that night's title / European / relegation odds

Model report card

How to read this
Every prediction the site publishes is written to a committed log the moment it is made, and frozen the instant a result exists — so this table grades calls that were on record before kickoff. That is a stricter test than the backtest, where the model's own settings were chosen by looking at the matches it is scored on. The Brier score is the squared error of the whole probability split, not just the top pick: 0 is perfect, 0.647 is what guessing each league's home/draw/away base rates gets you, and the backtest average is 0.583. Calibration is the more revealing half of the table — a model can pick winners at a mediocre rate and still be well calibrated, which is what makes its probabilities usable. Once some calls have been revised between publication and kickoff, a further row re-scores the same fixtures using the first call the site ever published for them; if that number is close to the main one, the extra fortnight of data adds less than you would think. The skill or luck table scores the very same calls a second time, against Understat's post-match simulation of each fixture instead of against its scoreline: the Brier a call would have earned on average had the match been replayed from the chances both sides created. It is the one number here that can tell a bad model from a bad night, and it is pooled across the five leagues Understat covers because per league there are nowhere near enough graded calls to read. It is not a rival forecast — Understat's number exists only after the final whistle and knows every shot that was taken, which is exactly what makes it a fair standard to be judged against and a useless one to predict with.
Far too early to mean anything. 20 graded calls is noise — a coin can look like a genius over ten matches. This table is here to fill up honestly over the season, not to be read yet.

For a fixture, the home side's expected goals are its attack scaled by the opponent's defence relative to the league average, times a home-advantage factor measured from the league's own home/away xG split — and the same, mirrored, for the visitors. Feeding both expectations through independent Poisson distributions gives a probability for every scoreline, summed into the win/draw/win split shown in the bar. xG f'cast is each side's expected goals — deliberately not turned into a predicted scoreline, because chance quality says little about which exact score a match lands on and even the favourite scoreline rarely tops 15%. In the Understat leagues a small territory term also scales each attack by the club's deep-completions rate relative to the league average — validated on held-out seasons, unlike pressing intensity (PPDA), which was tried the same way, carried no extra signal, and stays out. Allsvenskan's feed has no deep-completions metric, so its model simply omits the term. Strengths reach back 1400 days — nearly four seasons — with that 180-day half-life doing the forgetting, a combination that beat a shorter hard-cutoff window on held-out seasons: an old match should fade, not fall off a cliff, because even faint evidence of how good a club is turns out to be worth keeping. Replaying every stored season with this exact recipe (backtest.py, 20,900 predictable matches) gives Brier 0.583 and 53% outcome accuracy, against 0.647 and 44% for guessing by league base rates.
A model, not a promise. These probabilities come from a small Poisson model over each club's recency-weighted chance quality (non-penalty xG, blended with a dash of actual goals) — nothing else. It has never heard of transfers, injuries, suspensions or new managers, and until the new season produces matches it leans heavily on last season's form. Clubs with no recent top-flight xG history at all have their fixtures left unpredicted. Backtested over 21,700 matches back to 2014/15 it calls the right result 53% of the time — clearly better than always guessing home win (44%), nowhere near clairvoyant. A conversation starter — never betting advice.

Season projection (2026-2027)

How to read this

What it does. Every fixture left in the season is played out 5,000 times using the same Poisson model as the predictions above, and the resulting final tables are counted up. Proj is the average final points total; the three percentages are how often a club finished first, in the top 4, and in the bottom 3.

Why it disagrees with the table. Points already banked are carried over untouched — they are real. Everything still to come is projected from recency-weighted non-penalty xG, which is mostly deaf to a hot finishing run. So a club sitting third on a thin xG record gets to keep its points and is still projected to fade, while a good side stuck in mid-table is projected to climb. The gap between the Now and # columns is that disagreement, in places.

Does it work? season_lab.py replays 58 finished seasons and projects the final table at ten points in each. Before a ball is kicked it lands 8.2 points per club from the final total; after a tenth of a season, 7.7 — against 18.8 for reading the table and multiplying, which at that stage is worse than simply assuming every club finishes on the league average. The model is ahead at every checkpoint right through to the final tenth, on held-out seasons its settings were never tuned on. Shrinking it back toward the table was tried and made it worse at every weight. Worth knowing: the preseason projection is already most of the way there. Updating it as results arrive is worth about 0.2 points per club after a tenth of the season, peaks near 0.7 at halfway, and is back under 0.2 by the run-in — most of what this table knows, it knew in August.

Reading the percentages. They are simulation frequencies, not certainties, and the top-four and bottom-three cuts are the site's own convention — real European and relegation places vary by league and by season. Anything under 0.5% shows as a dash.

Form, not news. The simulation knows only what clubs have done on the pitch. It has never heard of a transfer window, a sacking or an injury — when those things matter, they reach the projection the slow way, through results. It also assumes each club's current level holds for the rest of the season, which is exactly the assumption a January collapse breaks. A club returning after a year in the division below is projected on the last top-flight football it played, which may be a squad ago. A club scoring far more than its chances suggest is only partly credited for it — usually the right call, since across 1,170 historical team-seasons that kind of overperformance mostly evaporates, but the extreme cases (Sirius-scale runs included) regressed to roughly half their gap rather than to zero, and the model's discount was never tuned specifically for that tail.

How wide is that projection?

How to read this

What it shows. The same 5,000 simulated seasons behind the Proj column above, but kept as a distribution of finishing positions instead of averaged down to one number. A short bar means the simulations agree; a long one means the run-in is still wide open for that club.

Reading it. The thick bar covers the middle half of simulated outcomes, the thin line the middle 90% — so a club whose thick bar sits entirely inside the shaded relegation band is in real trouble, while one whose bar straddles the line is still fighting it. The tick is the median finish, which is usually close to but not identical to the rounded Proj points figure above (points and rank are different simulation outputs).

Simulate one season

How to read this

What it does. Click the button and every fixture still to be played gets one simulated scoreline — each team's goals drawn from a Poisson distribution around the same expected-goals number (lam_home/lam_away) used everywhere else on this page — then the final table is built from real goals this time, not just win/draw/loss margins, so goal difference and the goals column are genuine tiebreakers rather than a coin flip. Click again for a different one.

Why it won't match the projection above. The Proj table is the average of thousands of these; any single run can and will put a mid-table side in the title race or drop a contender to mid-table, the same way any one real season can. That's the point of running it once instead of a thousand times — it shows what a plausible individual outcome actually looks like, not just the odds of it.

Plays every remaining fixture once, using the same expected-goals numbers as the projection above.

Projection over time

How to read this

What it shows. The season projection above is recomputed from scratch on every build, so on its own the page can only ever show tonight's opinion. This is every previous night's opinion too — one point added per team per night the projection ran, going back to the first snapshot logged this season.

Reading it. The number is projected final points, not the live table — it moves for two different reasons that look identical on the curve: a result banking real points, or the model simply revising its opinion of a club's remaining fixtures without a ball being kicked. Hover any dot for that night's title, European and relegation odds, which move for the same two reasons.

Why not just show probabilities. Title, European and relegation odds are usually a flat 0% or 100% for most of a season for most clubs — a true story for a handful of teams and a flat line for everyone else. Projected points moves for every club, contending or not, which is why it is the line and the odds are the hover.

Model report card

How to read this
Every prediction the site publishes is written to a committed log the moment it is made, and frozen the instant a result exists — so this table grades calls that were on record before kickoff. That is a stricter test than the backtest, where the model's own settings were chosen by looking at the matches it is scored on. The Brier score is the squared error of the whole probability split, not just the top pick: 0 is perfect, 0.647 is what guessing each league's home/draw/away base rates gets you, and the backtest average is 0.583. Calibration is the more revealing half of the table — a model can pick winners at a mediocre rate and still be well calibrated, which is what makes its probabilities usable. Once some calls have been revised between publication and kickoff, a further row re-scores the same fixtures using the first call the site ever published for them; if that number is close to the main one, the extra fortnight of data adds less than you would think. The skill or luck table scores the very same calls a second time, against Understat's post-match simulation of each fixture instead of against its scoreline: the Brier a call would have earned on average had the match been replayed from the chances both sides created. It is the one number here that can tell a bad model from a bad night, and it is pooled across the five leagues Understat covers because per league there are nowhere near enough graded calls to read. It is not a rival forecast — Understat's number exists only after the final whistle and knows every shot that was taken, which is exactly what makes it a fair standard to be judged against and a useless one to predict with.
Far too early to mean anything. 18 graded calls is noise — a coin can look like a genius over ten matches. This table is here to fill up honestly over the season, not to be read yet.

How to read this
Each club gets an attack and defence strength: a recency-weighted blend of 70% non-penalty xG and 30% actual goals, for and against (a match 180 days old counts half as much as one today — penalties are mostly noise, while real goals carry a club's persistent finishing skill). In the Understat leagues a small territory term also scales each attack by the club's deep-completions rate relative to the league average — validated on held-out seasons, unlike pressing intensity (PPDA), which was tried the same way, carried no extra signal, and stays out. Allsvenskan's feed has no deep-completions metric, so its model simply omits the term. Strengths reach back 1400 days — nearly four seasons — with that 180-day half-life doing the forgetting, a combination that beat a shorter hard-cutoff window on held-out seasons: an old match should fade, not fall off a cliff, because even faint evidence of how good a club is turns out to be worth keeping. Replaying every stored season with this exact recipe (backtest.py, 20,900 predictable matches) gives Brier 0.583 and 53% outcome accuracy, against 0.647 and 44% for guessing by league base rates.
A model, not a promise. These probabilities come from a small Poisson model over each club's recency-weighted chance quality (non-penalty xG, blended with a dash of actual goals) — nothing else. It has never heard of transfers, injuries, suspensions or new managers, and until the new season produces matches it leans heavily on last season's form. Clubs with no recent top-flight xG history at all have their fixtures left unpredicted. Backtested over 21,700 matches back to 2014/15 it calls the right result 53% of the time — clearly better than always guessing home win (44%), nowhere near clairvoyant. Model report card

How to read this
Every prediction the site publishes is written to a committed log the moment it is made, and frozen the instant a result exists — so this table grades calls that were on record before kickoff. That is a stricter test than the backtest, where the model's own settings were chosen by looking at the matches it is scored on. The Brier score is the squared error of the whole probability split, not just the top pick: 0 is perfect, 0.647 is what guessing each league's home/draw/away base rates gets you, and the backtest average is 0.583. Calibration is the more revealing half of the table — a model can pick winners at a mediocre rate and still be well calibrated, which is what makes its probabilities usable. Once some calls have been revised between publication and kickoff, a further row re-scores the same fixtures using the first call the site ever published for them; if that number is close to the main one, the extra fortnight of data adds less than you would think. The skill or luck table scores the very same calls a second time, against Understat's post-match simulation of each fixture instead of against its scoreline: the Brier a call would have earned on average had the match been replayed from the chances both sides created. It is the one number here that can tell a bad model from a bad night, and it is pooled across the five leagues Understat covers because per league there are nowhere near enough graded calls to read. It is not a rival forecast — Understat's number exists only after the final whistle and knows every shot that was taken, which is exactly what makes it a fair standard to be judged against and a useless one to predict with.
Far too early to mean anything. 25 graded calls is noise — a coin can look like a genius over ten matches. This table is here to fill up honestly over the season, not to be read yet.

Predictions (xG Poisson model)

How to read this
Each club gets an attack and defence strength: a recency-weighted blend of 70% non-penalty xG and 30% actual goals, for and against (a match 180 days old counts half as much as one today — penalties are mostly noise, while real goals carry a club's persistent finishing skill). For a fixture, the home side's expected goals are its attack scaled by the opponent's defence relative to the league average, times a home-advantage factor measured from the league's own home/away xG split — and the same, mirrored, for the visitors. Feeding both expectations through independent Poisson distributions gives a probability for every scoreline, summed into the win/draw/win split shown in the bar. xG f'cast is each side's expected goals — deliberately not turned into a predicted scoreline, because chance quality says little about which exact score a match lands on and even the favourite scoreline rarely tops 15%. In the Understat leagues a small territory term also scales each attack by the club's deep-completions rate relative to the league average — validated on held-out seasons, unlike pressing intensity (PPDA), which was tried the same way, carried no extra signal, and stays out. Allsvenskan's feed has no deep-completions metric, so its model simply omits the term. Strengths reach back 1400 days — nearly four seasons — with that 180-day half-life doing the forgetting, a combination that beat a shorter hard-cutoff window on held-out seasons: an old match should fade, not fall off a cliff, because even faint evidence of how good a club is turns out to be worth keeping. Replaying every stored season with this exact recipe (backtest.py, 20,900 predictable matches) gives Brier 0.583 and 53% outcome accuracy, against 0.647 and 44% for guessing by league base rates.
A model, not a promise. These probabilities come from a small Poisson model over each club's recency-weighted chance quality (non-penalty xG, blended with a dash of actual goals) — nothing else. It has never heard of transfers, injuries, suspensions or new managers, and until the new season produces matches it leans heavily on last season's form. Clubs with no recent top-flight xG history at all have their fixtures left unpredicted. Backtested over 21,700 matches back to 2014/15 it calls the right result 53% of the time — clearly better than always guessing home win (44%), nowhere near clairvoyant. A conversation starter — never betting advice.

Season projection (2026-2027)

How to read this

What it does. Every fixture left in the season is played out 5,000 times using the same Poisson model as the predictions above, and the resulting final tables are counted up. Proj is the average final points total; the three percentages are how often a club finished first, in the top 4, and in the bottom 3.

Why it disagrees with the table. Points already banked are carried over untouched — they are real. Everything still to come is projected from recency-weighted non-penalty xG, which is mostly deaf to a hot finishing run. So a club sitting third on a thin xG record gets to keep its points and is still projected to fade, while a good side stuck in mid-table is projected to climb. The gap between the Now and # columns is that disagreement, in places.

Does it work? season_lab.py replays 58 finished seasons and projects the final table at ten points in each. Before a ball is kicked it lands 8.2 points per club from the final total; after a tenth of a season, 7.7 — against 18.8 for reading the table and multiplying, which at that stage is worse than simply assuming every club finishes on the league average. The model is ahead at every checkpoint right through to the final tenth, on held-out seasons its settings were never tuned on. Shrinking it back toward the table was tried and made it worse at every weight. Worth knowing: the preseason projection is already most of the way there. Updating it as results arrive is worth about 0.2 points per club after a tenth of the season, peaks near 0.7 at halfway, and is back under 0.2 by the run-in — most of what this table knows, it knew in August.

Reading the percentages. They are simulation frequencies, not certainties, and the top-four and bottom-three cuts are the site's own convention — real European and relegation places vary by league and by season. Anything under 0.5% shows as a dash.

Form, not news. The simulation knows only what clubs have done on the pitch. It has never heard of a transfer window, a sacking or an injury — when those things matter, they reach the projection the slow way, through results. It also assumes each club's current level holds for the rest of the season, which is exactly the assumption a January collapse breaks. A club returning after a year in the division below is projected on the last top-flight football it played, which may be a squad ago. A club scoring far more than its chances suggest is only partly credited for it — usually the right call, since across 1,170 historical team-seasons that kind of overperformance mostly evaporates, but the extreme cases (Sirius-scale runs included) regressed to roughly half their gap rather than to zero, and the model's discount was never tuned specifically for that tail.

297 of 306 matches left to play. Points already won are kept as they are; every remaining fixture is simulated from current xG form.

How wide is that projection?

How to read this

What it shows. The same 5,000 simulated seasons behind the Proj column above, but kept as a distribution of finishing positions instead of averaged down to one number. A short bar means the simulations agree; a long one means the run-in is still wide open for that club.

Reading it. The thick bar covers the middle half of simulated outcomes, the thin line the middle 90% — so a club whose thick bar sits entirely inside the shaded relegation band is in real trouble, while one whose bar straddles the line is still fighting it. The tick is the median finish, which is usually close to but not identical to the rounded Proj points figure above (points and rank are different simulation outputs).

Simulate one season

How to read this

What it does. Click the button and every fixture still to be played gets one simulated scoreline — each team's goals drawn from a Poisson distribution around the same expected-goals number (lam_home/lam_away) used everywhere else on this page — then the final table is built from real goals this time, not just win/draw/loss margins, so goal difference and the goals column are genuine tiebreakers rather than a coin flip. Click again for a different one.

Why it won't match the projection above. The Proj table is the average of thousands of these; any single run can and will put a mid-table side in the title race or drop a contender to mid-table, the same way any one real season can. That's the point of running it once instead of a thousand times — it shows what a plausible individual outcome actually looks like, not just the odds of it.

Plays every remaining fixture once, using the same expected-goals numbers as the projection above.

Projection over time

How to read this

What it shows. The season projection above is recomputed from scratch on every build, so on its own the page can only ever show tonight's opinion. This is every previous night's opinion too — one point added per team per night the projection ran, going back to the first snapshot logged this season.

Reading it. The number is projected final points, not the live table — it moves for two different reasons that look identical on the curve: a result banking real points, or the model simply revising its opinion of a club's remaining fixtures without a ball being kicked. Hover any dot for that night's title, European and relegation odds, which move for the same two reasons.

Why not just show probabilities. Title, European and relegation odds are usually a flat 0% or 100% for most of a season for most clubs — a true story for a handful of teams and a flat line for everyone else. Projected points moves for every club, contending or not, which is why it is the line and the odds are the hover.

Allsvenskan's feed has no deep-completions metric, so its model simply omits the term. Strengths reach back 1400 days — nearly four seasons — with that 180-day half-life doing the forgetting, a combination that beat a shorter hard-cutoff window on held-out seasons: an old match should fade, not fall off a cliff, because even faint evidence of how good a club is turns out to be worth keeping. Replaying every stored season with this exact recipe (backtest.py, 20,900 predictable matches) gives Brier 0.583 and 53% outcome accuracy, against 0.647 and 44% for guessing by league base rates.
A model, not a promise. These probabilities come from a small Poisson model over each club's recency-weighted chance quality (non-penalty xG, blended with a dash of actual goals) — nothing else. It has never heard of transfers, injuries, suspensions or new managers, and until the new season produces matches it leans heavily on last season's form. Clubs with no recent top-flight xG history at all have their fixtures left unpredicted. Backtested over 21,700 matches back to 2014/15 it calls the right result 53% of the time — clearly better than always guessing home win (44%), nowhere near clairvoyant. A conversation starter — never betting advice.

Season projection (2026-2027)

How to read this

What it does. Every fixture left in the season is played out 5,000 times using the same Poisson model as the predictions above, and the resulting final tables are counted up. Proj is the average final points total; the three percentages are how often a club finished first, in the top 4, and in the bottom 3.

Why it disagrees with the table. Points already banked are carried over untouched — they are real. Everything still to come is projected from recency-weighted non-penalty xG, which is mostly deaf to a hot finishing run. So a club sitting third on a thin xG record gets to keep its points and is still projected to fade, while a good side stuck in mid-table is projected to climb. The gap between the Now and # columns is that disagreement, in places.

Does it work? season_lab.py replays 58 finished seasons and projects the final table at ten points in each. Before a ball is kicked it lands 8.2 points per club from the final total; after a tenth of a season, 7.7 — against 18.8 for reading the table and multiplying, which at that stage is worse than simply assuming every club finishes on the league average. The model is ahead at every checkpoint right through to the final tenth, on held-out seasons its settings were never tuned on. Shrinking it back toward the table was tried and made it worse at every weight. Worth knowing: the preseason projection is already most of the way there. Updating it as results arrive is worth about 0.2 points per club after a tenth of the season, peaks near 0.7 at halfway, and is back under 0.2 by the run-in — most of what this table knows, it knew in August.

Reading the percentages. They are simulation frequencies, not certainties, and the top-four and bottom-three cuts are the site's own convention — real European and relegation places vary by league and by season. Anything under 0.5% shows as a dash.

Form, not news. The simulation knows only what clubs have done on the pitch. It has never heard of a transfer window, a sacking or an injury — when those things matter, they reach the projection the slow way, through results. It also assumes each club's current level holds for the rest of the season, which is exactly the assumption a January collapse breaks. A club returning after a year in the division below is projected on the last top-flight football it played, which may be a squad ago. A club scoring far more than its chances suggest is only partly credited for it — usually the right call, since across 1,170 historical team-seasons that kind of overperformance mostly evaporates, but the extreme cases (Sirius-scale runs included) regressed to roughly half their gap rather than to zero, and the model's discount was never tuned specifically for that tail.

How wide is that projection?

How to read this

What it shows. The same 5,000 simulated seasons behind the Proj column above, but kept as a distribution of finishing positions instead of averaged down to one number. A short bar means the simulations agree; a long one means the run-in is still wide open for that club.

Reading it. The thick bar covers the middle half of simulated outcomes, the thin line the middle 90% — so a club whose thick bar sits entirely inside the shaded relegation band is in real trouble, while one whose bar straddles the line is still fighting it. The tick is the median finish, which is usually close to but not identical to the rounded Proj points figure above (points and rank are different simulation outputs).

Simulate one season

How to read this

What it does. Click the button and every fixture still to be played gets one simulated scoreline — each team's goals drawn from a Poisson distribution around the same expected-goals number (lam_home/lam_away) used everywhere else on this page — then the final table is built from real goals this time, not just win/draw/loss margins, so goal difference and the goals column are genuine tiebreakers rather than a coin flip. Click again for a different one.

Why it won't match the projection above. The Proj table is the average of thousands of these; any single run can and will put a mid-table side in the title race or drop a contender to mid-table, the same way any one real season can. That's the point of running it once instead of a thousand times — it shows what a plausible individual outcome actually looks like, not just the odds of it.

Plays every remaining fixture once, using the same expected-goals numbers as the projection above.

Projection over time

How to read this

What it shows. The season projection above is recomputed from scratch on every build, so on its own the page can only ever show tonight's opinion. This is every previous night's opinion too — one point added per team per night the projection ran, going back to the first snapshot logged this season.

Reading it. The number is projected final points, not the live table — it moves for two different reasons that look identical on the curve: a result banking real points, or the model simply revising its opinion of a club's remaining fixtures without a ball being kicked. Hover any dot for that night's title, European and relegation odds, which move for the same two reasons.

Why not just show probabilities. Title, European and relegation odds are usually a flat 0% or 100% for most of a season for most clubs — a true story for a handful of teams and a flat line for everyone else. Projected points moves for every club, contending or not, which is why it is the line and the odds are the hover.

Model report card

How to read this
Every prediction the site publishes is written to a committed log the moment it is made, and frozen the instant a result exists — so this table grades calls that were on record before kickoff. That is a stricter test than the backtest, where the model's own settings were chosen by looking at the matches it is scored on. The Brier score is the squared error of the whole probability split, not just the top pick: 0 is perfect, 0.647 is what guessing each league's home/draw/away base rates gets you, and the backtest average is 0.583. Calibration is the more revealing half of the table — a model can pick winners at a mediocre rate and still be well calibrated, which is what makes its probabilities usable. Once some calls have been revised between publication and kickoff, a further row re-scores the same fixtures using the first call the site ever published for them; if that number is close to the main one, the extra fortnight of data adds less than you would think. The skill or luck table scores the very same calls a second time, against Understat's post-match simulation of each fixture instead of against its scoreline: the Brier a call would have earned on average had the match been replayed from the chances both sides created. It is the one number here that can tell a bad model from a bad night, and it is pooled across the five leagues Understat covers because per league there are nowhere near enough graded calls to read. It is not a rival forecast — Understat's number exists only after the final whistle and knows every shot that was taken, which is exactly what makes it a fair standard to be judged against and a useless one to predict with.
Far too early to mean anything. 17 graded calls is noise — a coin can look like a genius over ten matches. This table is here to fill up honestly over the season, not to be read yet.

Predictions (xG Poisson model)

How to read this
Each club gets an attack and defence strength: a recency-weighted blend of 70% non-penalty xG and 30% actual goals, for and against (a match 180 days old counts half as much as one today — penalties are mostly noise, while real goals carry a club's persistent finishing skill). For a fixture, the home side's expected goals are its attack scaled by the opponent's defence relative to the league average, times a home-advantage factor measured from the league's own home/away xG split — and the same, mirrored, for the visitors. Feeding both expectations through independent Poisson distributions gives a probability for every scoreline, summed into the win/draw/win split shown in the bar. xG f'cast is each side's expected goals — deliberately not turned into a predicted scoreline, because chance quality says little about which exact score a match lands on and even the favourite scoreline rarely tops 15%. In the Understat leagues a small territory term also scales each attack by the club's deep-completions rate relative to the league average — validated on held-out seasons, unlike pressing intensity (PPDA), which was tried the same way, carried no extra signal, and stays out. Allsvenskan's feed has no deep-completions metric, so its model simply omits the term. Strengths reach back 1400 days — nearly four seasons — with that 180-day half-life doing the forgetting, a combination that beat a shorter hard-cutoff window on held-out seasons: an old match should fade, not fall off a cliff, because even faint evidence of how good a club is turns out to be worth keeping. Replaying every stored season with this exact recipe (backtest.py, 20,900 predictable matches) gives Brier 0.583 and 53% outcome accuracy, against 0.647 and 44% for guessing by league base rates.
A model, not a promise. These probabilities come from a small Poisson model over each club's recency-weighted chance quality (non-penalty xG, blended with a dash of actual goals) — nothing else. It has never heard of transfers, injuries, suspensions or new managers, and until the new season produces matches it leans heavily on last season's form. Clubs with no recent top-flight xG history at all have their fixtures left unpredicted. Backtested over 21,700 matches back to 2014/15 it calls the right result 53% of the time — clearly better than always guessing home win (44%), nowhere near clairvoyant. A conversation starter — never betting advice.

That is a stricter test than the backtest, where the model's own settings were chosen by looking at the matches it is scored on. The Brier score is the squared error of the whole probability split, not just the top pick: 0 is perfect, 0.647 is what guessing each league's home/draw/away base rates gets you, and the backtest average is 0.583. Calibration is the more revealing half of the table — a model can pick winners at a mediocre rate and still be well calibrated, which is what makes its probabilities usable. Once some calls have been revised between publication and kickoff, a further row re-scores the same fixtures using the first call the site ever published for them; if that number is close to the main one, the extra fortnight of data adds less than you would think. The skill or luck table scores the very same calls a second time, against Understat's post-match simulation of each fixture instead of against its scoreline: the Brier a call would have earned on average had the match been replayed from the chances both sides created. It is the one number here that can tell a bad model from a bad night, and it is pooled across the five leagues Understat covers because per league there are nowhere near enough graded calls to read. It is not a rival forecast — Understat's number exists only after the final whistle and knows every shot that was taken, which is exactly what makes it a fair standard to be judged against and a useless one to predict with.
A live scorecard, not the backtest. Every row here was published before kickoff and never edited, so unlike the backtest it cannot flatter the model with hindsight. Expect it to wander well above and below the backtested 53% for most of a season — a few hundred matches is still a small sample.

Matches

Pick an upcoming fixture to see both clubs side by side, or a match already played to see the score, what the chances were worth, and what the model said about it beforehand.

Match explorer

How to read this

What it shows. One match at a time, in either tense. An upcoming fixture gets everything the site knows about the two clubs gathered in one place: the model's win/draw/win call, both sides' recent form in results and in chance quality, their past meetings, the venue split that actually applies to this match, and each squad's leading attackers.

A match already played gets a report instead: the score, what the chances were worth on the day, and — the part worth coming for — what this site said about it beforehand, taken from the call written down before kickoff and never edited since. It is marked called it or missed on the day's actual result. A match that was never in a predictions slate says so rather than inventing a retrospective opinion; that is usually a promoted club with no top-flight xG history at the time. Form and squad lists are deliberately left off a report — they would describe the clubs now, not as they were then.

Match stats on a report are the team stat line both feeds keep for the 90 minutes, which is more than the xG the report used to show on its own. In the big five that is expected goals, non-penalty xG, deep completions (passes completed within about 20 metres of goal — territory rather than chances), PPDA (opposition passes allowed per defensive action: lower means more pressing, so its bar deliberately favours the smaller number) and expected points. Allsvenskan's feed measures far more, so its headline rows are expected goals, non-penalty xG, xG on target (which rates the shot rather than the chance, counting where in the goal it went), shots, shots on target, possession and expected points — with everything else the feed measured behind a disclosure under them: big chances and big chances missed, touches in the opposition box, xG split into open play and set play, corners, shots inside and outside the box, the woodwork, passes and pass accuracy, offsides, tackles, interceptions, blocks, clearances, keeper saves, duels and aerial duels won, successful dribbles, fouls and cards. The rows differ by league rather than being padded with blanks. The bar carries the comparison and the bolder number is the side ahead — except on the rows nobody wins, which are drawn faint and unbolded: tackles, blocks, clearances, saves, fouls and cards all climb with time spent defending, so a side can lead every one of them and be losing. Neither feed stores anything player-level per match, so there are no individual match ratings here; the player numbers on this site are season totals. A measurement neither side has is left off rather than printed empty — FotMob's xG on target is missing for whole matches at a time — and one only the away side has shows the home side a dash. A stat line that disagrees with the scoreline is dropped rather than shown: the two feeds would be describing different 90 minutes.

Where the shots came from is Allsvenskan only as well. FotMob records every attempt with the spot it was struck from and what a chance from there is worth, and each team gets its own picture of the last 36 metres of the pitch — which holds all but a handful of shots a season — both drawn attacking upwards. One circle is one shot and its area is its expected goals, so a circle twice as wide was four times the chance, down to a floor that keeps the faintest half-chances big enough to see: filled for a goal, filled paler for a save, grey where a defender blocked it, red where it hit the woodwork, and hollow for one that missed. The caption counts the shots, the ones on target and the expected goals they add up to. That last one can sit a little above the expected goals in the stat table, and the gap is not a mistake: FotMob discounts a shot taken straight after a save in the same passage of play, on the grounds that the chance has been counted once already, and adding the circles up one at a time does not. Hovering a circle names the player, the minute, the body part and what came of it; clicking one opens the same season card a name in the squad does. A shot from further out than the picture goes is drawn on its bottom edge rather than left out. Own goals are not on it at all — the feed records them at the other end of the pitch, under the man who scored one, with no expected goals — so they are counted in the caption of the team they were given to instead.

Who played is Allsvenskan only, and it is the one thing that league gets which the big five do not: FotMob keeps a stat line per player per match, Understat keeps none at all. Both squads are listed as they were used — starters first, then whoever came off the bench — with FotMob’s rating out of 10, minutes, goals, assists, expected goals and assists, and shots, all for that match alone. Goalkeepers get their own line underneath for saves and goals prevented, which is xG on target faced minus goals conceded: a positive number is a keeper who saved more than the shots deserved. A name opens that player’s season card where the page holds one, because the match feed and the season squads share FotMob’s player ids and need no name matching. Anyone who did not get on is left out rather than listed with a dash.

The head-to-head on a report stops before the match being reported, so it shows the history the two sides actually brought into it.

The verdict is the same Poisson model as the Predictions block on the League tab, reading from the same numbers — the two can never disagree about a match. Its caveats apply here in full: no transfers, no injuries, no suspensions, no new managers.

Form is the last six matches, newest first, with the score and both sides' xG that day. It deliberately reaches back across the summer rather than showing an empty strip in August — a club's last six competitive matches are still the best short-term evidence there is, even if some were played in May. By venue shows each club at the venue it will actually be at — the home side's home record against the visitors' away record — with its record across all matches underneath, because a side that is excellent at home and ordinary overall is exactly the case the venue row alone would hide. Both cover a single season, named in the heading. In August that is still last season for a club that has not kicked off yet, and the two sides of a fixture can even be anchored to different seasons; the heading says which rather than calling it all 'this season'. The same goes for leading attackers, labelled per club, which falls back to the last completed season until this one has enough minutes in it to mean anything.

Head-to-head reaches back as far as the xG data goes — up to twelve seasons — and gives each meeting's score alongside what the chances were worth. A club that keeps losing these while winning the xG is a different story from one that is simply outplayed. It is kept deliberately neutral: no win/loss colouring, because this is the two clubs' shared history rather than a run of form belonging to whichever side happens to be at home this time — the winner of each meeting is marked on its name, and the tally names both clubs. Meetings in other competitions are not here; this is league data only.

What's missing is marked. A promoted club has no top-flight xG history, so the model declines to predict its fixtures rather than inventing a number, and its form and head-to-head sections say so instead of showing an empty table.

Preseason (club friendlies, FotMob)

Summer friendlies for the league's clubs — recent scores and the upcoming schedule. This tab only appears while friendlies are being played; once the season proper is under way it retires itself.

Friendlies lie. Preseason matches are played with rotated line-ups, experimental shapes and one eye on fitness — the results say little about the season ahead, and FotMob publishes no xG for them. This tab is for keeping an eye on what the clubs are up to over the summer, nothing more.

Team analytics (2026/27, Understat · Allsvenskan 2026, FotMob)

Metric glossary — what xG, npxG, xGBuildup, PPDA and friends actually mean
xG — expected goals
How good a team's or player's chances were. Every shot gets a value between 0 and 1: the probability that an average player scores from that spot and situation. A tap-in is ~0.9, a hopeful 30-metre hit ~0.02. Add them up and you get how many goals the chances “should” have produced.
xA — expected assists
The same idea for passing: the xG of the shot a pass created. A player who keeps serving up big chances gets a high xA even if teammates keep missing them.
npxG / npg — non-penalty xG and goals
xG and goals with penalties removed. A penalty is worth ~0.76 xG no matter who wins it, so stripping them out shows how much a player or team creates from open play.
G−xG — finishing
Goals scored minus expected goals. Above zero: converting chances an average finisher would miss. Below zero: missing chances that usually go in. Tends to swing back toward zero over time.
KP — key passes
Passes that led directly to a shot, whether or not it went in. Raw creativity volume, where xA measures the quality of what was created.
xGChain (xGCh)
Credit for being anywhere in a move that ended in a shot: the full xG of the chance is credited to every player who touched the ball in the build-up. Rewards involvement, not just the final pass or shot.
xGBuildup (xGB)
xGChain minus the shot and the assist pass. What's left is pure build-up play — deep-lying passers and defenders who start attacks score high here even with zero goals and assists.
PPDA — pressing intensity
Opponent passes allowed per defensive action in their half. Counter-intuitive direction: a LOW number means an aggressive press (the opponent barely gets 10 passes before being tackled), a high number means the team sits back.
Deep completions
Passes received within roughly 20 metres of the opponent's goal (crosses excluded). A good measure of sustained territory and box presence.
xPts — expected points
How many points a match “should” have given based on both teams' chances: the chance quality is converted into win/draw/loss probabilities and summed over the season. A team far above its xPts has been winning tight or lucky games.
npxGD — underlying dominance
Non-penalty xG created minus non-penalty xG conceded, per match. The single best summary of how well a team actually played, ignoring finishing luck at both ends.

xG table — results vs expected

How to read this

What it shows. Results next to what the chances say they should have been. xG (expected goals) values every shot by how often that kind of chance is scored; xPts converts each match's shots into win/draw/loss probabilities and sums the expected points.

How to read it. Pts−xPts above zero means the team banked more points than its chances deserved — running hot on finishing, goalkeeping or timing. npxGD is non-penalty xG difference (created minus conceded), widely considered the best single number for underlying strength: it predicts future results better than points do.

Caveat. xG is a model of chance quality, not truth — elite finishers beat it consistently, and one season is a small sample.

xG table — results vs expected

How to read this

What it shows. Results next to what the chances say they should have been. xG (expected goals) values every shot by how often that kind of chance is scored; xPts converts each match's shots into win/draw/loss probabilities and sums the expected points.

How to read it. Pts−xPts above zero means the team banked more points than its chances deserved — running hot on finishing, goalkeeping or timing. npxGD is non-penalty xG difference (created minus conceded), widely considered the best single number for underlying strength: it predicts future results better than points do.

Caveat. xG is a model of chance quality, not truth — elite finishers beat it consistently, and one season is a small sample.

Team comparison

How to read this

What it shows. One to three teams overlaid on a radar of six style dimensions, each expressed as the team's percentile among the sides in that league. A single team is a profile rather than a comparison — that is where a click on a club's name over on the League tab lands, and it carries the club's last six matches underneath, because the radar says what kind of side this is and only the results say how it is going. Attack is non-penalty xG created per match and Defence is non-penalty xG conceded (flipped, so further out = fewer chances allowed). Finishing is goals minus xG — conversion above or below what the chances deserved. Pressing is PPDA flipped (opponent passes allowed per defensive action — fewer means a higher press). Territory is deep completions per match (passes received within ~20m of the opponent goal) and Box defence is the same thing conceded, flipped.

How to read it. The shape is the identity: a dominant pressing side bulges toward Attack–Pressing–Territory, a low-block counter team can look small here yet still win points on Finishing and Box defence. The table underneath gives the raw per-match numbers behind each axis, plus points vs expected points. Shots on target aren't in the data — Understat's team feed doesn't publish them — so chance quality (xG) stands in for shot accuracy.

Season by season. Under a single club, one row per season as far back as the data goes — where they finished, the record, goal difference, xG difference, and points against expected points. The bar is the gap between those last two: right and green means the club banked more than its chances deserved, left and red means it banked fewer. It is the luck quadrant from the Insights tab asked of a decade instead of a season, and it is what says whether a good year was a step up or a hot streak. A season spent in a lower division shows as a gap rather than being skipped, so the relegations are visible too. One caveat: the position is computed from the stored results, so it does not know about points deductions — Everton and Nottingham Forest in 2023/24, and Juventus in 2022/23, finished lower than this table puts them.

The squad. Under a single club, everyone who has played a minute for it in the season the page is about, most minutes first, with goals against xG and assists against xA. It lists players used, not a registered squad — neither feed carries a player until they have appeared — so a club one matchday into a season shows the eleven and its substitutes and grows to the mid-twenties by May. In the big five a name opens that player's profile card and career underneath; Allsvenskan's squads come from FotMob, which publishes no positions and nothing the player explorer is built on, so those names are listed rather than linked. It costs the page nothing in the big five — those players are already loaded for the Players tab, so the squad is a filter over them rather than a second copy.

Head-to-head mode. With exactly two teams picked, the card goes deeper: a tale-of-the-tape strip where each bar is split by the two sides' league-percentile share (the longer half leads, the number in brackets is the league rank as a percentile ordinal), this season's actual meetings between the clubs with the score and each side's xG that day, the last five results, points and non-penalty xG difference split by home/away, and both teams' rolling 6-match npxGD form curves overlaid on one chart — so you can see not just who is better on the season, but who is better right now, and what happened when they actually met.

Pick a team above for its style profile and recent form, or two or three to see them side by side. Picking exactly two unlocks a head-to-head deep dive: this season's meetings, a tale-of-the-tape bar duel, recent form, home/away splits and overlaid form curves.

Team style — pressing vs territory

How to read this

What it shows. Each team's playing identity in two numbers, averaged over the season. PPDA (passes per defensive action) counts how many passes a team lets the opponent play before making a tackle, interception or foul — fewer means a more aggressive press. Deep completions are passes completed within roughly 20 metres of the opponent's goal — a proxy for sustained territorial dominance.

How to read it. Top-left teams press high and pin opponents into their own box — the modern dominant style. Bottom-right teams sit deep and play direct, ceding the ball and the territory. Neither corner is 'better' — it's a style map, not a quality ranking. Hover a dot for exact values.

Form curves — rolling xG difference

How to read this

What it shows. Every team's underlying form across the whole season: non-penalty xG difference (chances created minus chances conceded, penalties excluded) averaged over a rolling 5-match window. Teams appear in final-table order and all curves share the same scale (±2.1), so shapes are directly comparable.

How to read it. Green stretches above the line are periods of outplaying opponents; red dips below are periods of being outplayed. Look for the story in the shape: a title challenge that faded after mid-season, a slow starter that clicked after a coaching change, a relegated team that was actually improving. The number after each name is the latest value; hover a curve for its season range.

Metric glossary — what xG, npxG, xGBuildup, PPDA and friends actually mean
xG — expected goals
How good a team's or player's chances were. Every shot gets a value between 0 and 1: the probability that an average player scores from that spot and situation. A tap-in is ~0.9, a hopeful 30-metre hit ~0.02. Add them up and you get how many goals the chances “should” have produced.
xA — expected assists
The same idea for passing: the xG of the shot a pass created. A player who keeps serving up big chances gets a high xA even if teammates keep missing them.
npxG / npg — non-penalty xG and goals
xG and goals with penalties removed. A penalty is worth ~0.76 xG no matter who wins it, so stripping them out shows how much a player or team creates from open play.
G−xG — finishing
Goals scored minus expected goals. Above zero: converting chances an average finisher would miss. Below zero: missing chances that usually go in. Tends to swing back toward zero over time.
KP — key passes
Passes that led directly to a shot, whether or not it went in. Raw creativity volume, where xA measures the quality of what was created.
xGChain (xGCh)
Credit for being anywhere in a move that ended in a shot: the full xG of the chance is credited to every player who touched the ball in the build-up. Rewards involvement, not just the final pass or shot.
xGBuildup (xGB)
xGChain minus the shot and the assist pass. What's left is pure build-up play — deep-lying passers and defenders who start attacks score high here even with zero goals and assists.
PPDA — pressing intensity
Opponent passes allowed per defensive action in their half. Counter-intuitive direction: a LOW number means an aggressive press (the opponent barely gets 10 passes before being tackled), a high number means the team sits back.
Deep completions
Passes received within roughly 20 metres of the opponent's goal (crosses excluded). A good measure of sustained territory and box presence.
xPts — expected points
How many points a match “should” have given based on both teams' chances: the chance quality is converted into win/draw/loss probabilities and summed over the season. A team far above its xPts has been winning tight or lucky games.
npxGD — underlying dominance
Non-penalty xG created minus non-penalty xG conceded, per match. The single best summary of how well a team actually played, ignoring finishing luck at both ends.

Player explorer

How to read this

What it shows. Every player Understat tracks in the selected league this season (1766 across the big five). The table starts with the top 25 by the current sort — use the buttons under it to load more. Search by name or club, filter by position and minutes, and click any column header to sort (click again to flip direction). Click a row to open that player's profile card, with season totals, percentile bars against players of the same position, and the whole career Understat has stored underneath.

The career strip. One row per season on the profile card, back to 2014/15, with the club, the minutes, goals against xG and assists against xA — so a season reads against the rest of the player's career rather than on its own. Moves draw themselves: a club in another league is labelled and dimmed, and a mid-season transfer leaves two rows under one season, ordered by minutes because the feed carries no dates to order them by. A season with no row is one Understat did not cover — it tracks the big five only, so a gap means a spell outside them (a second division, a league elsewhere), not a year out of football. The bar is goals minus xG, which over a career is the difference between a finisher having one hot season and being a good finisher.

The columns. xG and xA are expected goals and expected assists — the value of the chances a player took or created. G−xG above zero means finishing better than the chances deserved; A−xA above zero means teammates converted the chances generously. KP is key passes (passes leading directly to a shot), npxG strips out penalties.

Per 90. The toggle converts volume stats to per-90-minute rates, which makes part-time players comparable to ever-presents — players under 270 minutes are hidden in that mode to avoid tiny-sample noise. Players transferred mid-season show both clubs, comma-separated.

Click a row for that player's profile card — season totals, per-90 percentiles against their peers, and every season stored for them.

Player comparison

How to read this

What it shows. Up to three players overlaid on a radar of six per-90 attacking dimensions — non-penalty expected goals (npxG: the value of the shots taken, penalties excluded), expected assists (xA: the value of the chances created), shots, key passes (passes leading to a shot), xGChain (involvement anywhere in a scoring move) and xGBuildup (build-up play only, shots and assists excluded — see the glossary at the top of this tab). Each axis is the player's percentile among players of the same position in their own league with 450+ minutes, so a defender isn't drowned by striker numbers; the table below gives the exact per-90 rates.

How to read it. The bigger the shape, the more complete the attacking contribution — but shape profile matters more than area: a pure finisher spikes toward npxG and shots, a creator toward xA and key passes, a deep engine toward xGBuildup. Comparing a striker with a full-back is fair here because each is measured against their own position group — and since the search spans all five leagues, cross-league match-ups work the same way: each player is ranked against their own league's peers, so the radar answers “who dominates their context more”, not who would outscore whom in the same league.

Pick two or three players above (or use “Add to comparison” on a player card) to see their profiles side by side. The search covers all five leagues, so cross-league match-ups work too.

Clinical finishers — most goals above xG

How to read this

What it shows. The players (≥900 minutes) whose goal tallies differ most from the value of their chances. G−xG is goals scored minus expected goals: far above zero means converting chances an average finisher would miss.

How to read it. A single hot season can be luck; players who beat their xG year after year are genuinely elite finishers. Check the shots column too — a big overshoot on few shots is far flukier than the same overshoot on a hundred.

PlayerTeamMinShotsGoalsxGG−xG

Wasteful in front of goal — most goals below xG

How to read this

What it shows. The other end of the list — players (≥900 minutes) who scored the fewest goals relative to the chances they had.

How to read it. This is not simply a wall of shame: a player here with a high xG is still getting into great positions, which is the hard part — finishing tends to bounce back. A player with low xG and a big negative gap has a real problem.

PlayerTeamMinShotsGoalsxGG−xG

Top creators by expected assists

How to read this

What it shows. The league's best chance creators (≥900 minutes), ranked by expected assists — the probability that the shots their passes created would be scored.

How to read it. xA measures the quality of the chance served, independent of whether the teammate buried it. A−xA below zero means the creator was let down by finishing; above zero means teammates converted generously. xA is the fairer ranking of creativity than raw assists.

How to read it. This is not simply a wall of shame: a player here with a high xG is still getting into great positions, which is the hard part — finishing tends to bounce back. A player with low xG and a big negative gap has a real problem.

Top creators by expected assists

How to read this

What it shows. The league's best chance creators (≥900 minutes), ranked by expected assists — the probability that the shots their passes created would be scored.

How to read it. xA measures the quality of the chance served, independent of whether the teammate buried it. A−xA below zero means the creator was let down by finishing; above zero means teammates converted generously. xA is the fairer ranking of creativity than raw assists.

How to read this

Where the numbers come from. Allsvenskan has no free Understat-style feed, so these stats come from FotMob (Opta data): xG, xA, shots, shots on target and chances created. xGChain, xGBuildup and per-player non-penalty xG aren't published there, which is why this league has curated boards instead of the full player explorer.

Insights (2026/27, Understat · Allsvenskan 2026, FotMob)

Second-order reads of the xG data: what the raw tables hide.

Metric glossary — what xG, npxG, xGBuildup, PPDA and friends actually mean
xG — expected goals
How good a team's or player's chances were. Every shot gets a value between 0 and 1: the probability that an average player scores from that spot and situation. A tap-in is ~0.9, a hopeful 30-metre hit ~0.02. Add them up and you get how many goals the chances “should” have produced.
xA — expected assists
The same idea for passing: the xG of the shot a pass created. A player who keeps serving up big chances gets a high xA even if teammates keep missing them.
npxG / npg — non-penalty xG and goals
xG and goals with penalties removed. A penalty is worth ~0.76 xG no matter who wins it, so stripping them out shows how much a player or team creates from open play.
G−xG — finishing
Goals scored minus expected goals. Above zero: converting chances an average finisher would miss. Below zero: missing chances that usually go in. Tends to swing back toward zero over time.
KP — key passes
Passes that led directly to a shot, whether or not it went in. Raw creativity volume, where xA measures the quality of what was created.
xGChain (xGCh)
Credit for being anywhere in a move that ended in a shot: the full xG of the chance is credited to every player who touched the ball in the build-up. Rewards involvement, not just the final pass or shot.
xGBuildup (xGB)
xGChain minus the shot and the assist pass. What's left is pure build-up play — deep-lying passers and defenders who start attacks score high here even with zero goals and assists.
PPDA — pressing intensity
Opponent passes allowed per defensive action in their half. Counter-intuitive direction: a LOW number means an aggressive press (the opponent barely gets 10 passes before being tackled), a high number means the team sits back.
Deep completions
Passes received within roughly 20 metres of the opponent's goal (crosses excluded). A good measure of sustained territory and box presence.
xPts — expected points
How many points a match “should” have given based on both teams' chances: the chance quality is converted into win/draw/loss probabilities and summed over the season. A team far above its xPts has been winning tight or lucky games.
npxGD — underlying dominance
Non-penalty xG created minus non-penalty xG conceded, per match. The single best summary of how well a team actually played, ignoring finishing luck at both ends.

The justice table — where the chances say you belonged

How to read this

What it shows. The league re-ranked by expected points. xPts turns each match's chances into win/draw/loss probabilities and sums the expected points — so this is the table with finishing luck, deflections and goalkeeping heroics stripped out. Stripes mark where the Champions League and relegation places would have gone.

How to read it. ▲ in the Fortune column means the team finished that many places higher in the real table than its chances deserved — a fortunate season likely to regress. ▼ means the table undersold them; those teams are the classic bounce-back picks for next season, and where the value hides in pre-season betting markets and predictions.
